findings.situation: A filer whose foreign interest or dividends were high-taxed, or who had export financing interest, may truthfully answer no because the help never says these count, but for the election this income counts as passive and the line needs yes.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 1: "However, for this purpose, passive income also includes (a) income subject to the special rule for high-taxed income, described later; and (b) certain export financing interest."
findings.why: The question says only "under the small-tax election rules", and the help says passive income is "mostly interest and dividends". Neither tells the filer that high-taxed income and export financing interest count as passive for this election. A filer who knows these items normally fall outside the passive category would answer no.

findings.situation: A filer whose creditable foreign taxes are over $300 ($600 joint), or who has foreign income that is not passive or was not reported on a qualified payee statement, answers yes because they would prefer to skip Form 1116.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 1: "This election is available only if you meet all of the following conditions. • All of your foreign source gross income was 'passive category income' ... • All the income and any foreign taxes paid on it were reported to you on a qualified payee statement ... • Your total creditable foreign taxes aren't more than $300 ($600 if married filing a joint return). This election isn't available to estates or trusts."
findings.why: The question and its help ask only whether the filer chooses the election and never state the eligibility conditions. An ineligible filer can truthfully answer yes, so the line records an election that the text does not allow.

findings.situation: A filer with a foreign tax carryover from an earlier year reads 'with no carryover to or from this election year' as asking whether they have no carryover, not as a consequence they accept, and answers no even though they may elect.
findings.source_text: i1116 pp. 1–2: "You can't carry over to or from any other year any foreign taxes paid or accrued in a tax year to which the election applies (but carryovers to and from other years are unaffected)."
findings.why: The phrase can be read as a factual condition (no carryover exists) or as an effect of electing (giving up carryovers). Under the two readings the same eligible filer gives different answers.

findings.situation: A filer has foreign tax on several 1099-DIV dividends; one dividend fails the holding-period rule and the rest are creditable, so the positive gate amount already holds only the creditable taxes left after reductions.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 2: 'Taxes on income or gain that aren't creditable because you don't meet the holding period requirement, as described in item 5 or 7 under Foreign Taxes Not Eligible for a Credit'; gate helper: 'Total creditable foreign taxes after required reductions'
findings.why: The help says 'Yes if the foreign taxes are creditable and the holding-period, related-payment and required foreign-tax reduction rules have all been met'. A filer whose taxes did not all meet the rules truthfully answers no, even though the remaining creditable taxes still qualify and the line needs yes. The text treats the failing taxes as non-creditable (deductible) items, not as a bar to the whole credit.

findings.situation: A filer who has not already taken the line 12 reductions out of the amount entered is asked whether the 'required foreign-tax reduction rules' have been 'satisfied'.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 2: 'You are still required to reduce the taxes available for credit by any amount you would have entered on line 12 of Form 1116.'
findings.why: The line 12 reduction lowers the amount; it is not a pass/fail test. One filer may answer yes because the rule can be applied to the amount, while another answers no because the amount was not reduced, or because a reduction applies at all. The question and help name the holding-period and related-payment rules without saying what they require, so the answer depends on how the filer reads the wording.

findings.situation: A filer whose foreign income and taxes were reported on a Schedule K-3 (Form 1065 or 1120-S), a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), or a substitute statement may answer no, because the help names only Forms 1099-INT and 1099-DIV.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S), or similar substitute statements."
findings.why: "Qualified payee statement" is a term of art that an ordinary filer can't define without the full list. The help names only two of the qualifying statements, so a filer holding a K-3, a 1041 K-1 or a substitute statement could truthfully answer no when the election condition is met, and the lines would wrongly treat the election as unavailable.

findings.situation: A filer whose creditable foreign taxes were reported on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), a Schedule K-3 (Form 1065 or 1120-S), or a substitute statement follows the help, enters only Form 1099-INT box 6 plus Form 1099-DIV box 7, and leaves those taxes out.
findings.source_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S), or similar substitute statements." and "Your total creditable foreign taxes aren't more than $300 ($600 if married filing a joint return)."
findings.why: The total must include all creditable foreign taxes from every qualified payee statement, but the help names only the two 1099 boxes. An undercount lowers the credit on Schedule 3 line 1 and can make the total look like it is within the $300/$600 limit when it is not.
